findings.title: Non-constant-time secret comparison and header lookup allows timing/array edge cases
findings.body: The webhook secret check uses `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. Header values can be arrays (e.g., duplicate headers), in which case the comparison will always be false/true in unexpected ways, and more importantly a plain `!==` string compare is vulnerable to timing attacks on the secret. A constant-time comparison (e.g., crypto.timingSafeEqual) should be used instead, and the header value should be normalized to a string before comparison.

findings.title: No rate limiting or method check on credential sync webhook
findings.body: The handler does not verify req.method (so GET/PUT/etc. are all accepted) and has no rate limiting. Combined with the weak secret comparison, this endpoint that creates/updates user credentials is more exposed to brute force or misuse than it should be for a sensitive, cross-tenant credential-writing endpoint.

findings.title: appId lookup mismatches credential.appId (slug vs appMetadata.slug) potentially inconsistent, and type cast assumptions
findings.body: `appMetadata.slug` is used for both `appId` filter and create, and `appMetadata.type` for `type`, but there is no validation that these fields exist/match the expected shape of app store metadata beyond a loose JS object check. If `appMetadata.type` is undefined (some metadata entries may lack `type`), the credential will be created with type `undefined`, silently breaking later type-based lookups used by CalendarService/VideoApiAdapter constructors (which key off `credential.type`).

findings.title: symmetricDecrypt called with empty key fallback can throw unclear errors or decrypt incorrectly
findings.body: `process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || ""` silently falls back to an empty string key if the env var is unset, even though APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED already requires both CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY to be set per constants.ts. If somehow unset at runtime (race/misconfiguration), this produces either a cryptic crypto error or a wrong decryption rather than a clear validation error at the top of the handler.

findings.title: Missing prisma import causes runtime ReferenceError
findings.body: The new code in `getClient` calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` but `prisma` is never imported in this file (no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`). This will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime whenever Salesforce credentials are refreshed, breaking the Salesforce calendar refresh flow entirely.

findings.title: Token refresh now happens unconditionally on every client creation, ignoring expiry/validity
findings.body: Previously `getClient` likely only refreshed when needed; now it unconditionally calls the Salesforce OAuth refresh endpoint every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed, for every API call (create/update/delete event, availability). This causes excessive refresh-token usage, potential rate limiting/token invalidation by Salesforce (refresh tokens can become single-use leading to race conditions on concurrent requests), and performance overhead on every operation.

findings.title: Removed error logging when refresh token response fails validation
findings.body: The original code logged `tokenResponse.error` and the raw MS response via console.error when `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse` failed. This diagnostic logging was removed when switching to `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` only throws a generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" error without surfacing the actual Zod error or API response, making production debugging of OAuth refresh failures much harder.

findings.title: Refresh token response mutated to literal string "refresh_token" when missing, risking credential corruption
findings.body: When `refresh_token` is absent from the response, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — a literal placeholder string rather than preserving the existing refresh token or leaving it undefined. If this value is persisted to the credential record (as several call sites do, e.g. salesforce/zoho CalendarService), it will overwrite a valid refresh token with the literal string "refresh_token", breaking future refresh attempts and effectively invalidating the credential silently.

findings.title: External credential-sync endpoint response shape not validated against call site expectations
findings.body: When app credential syncing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw fetch `Response` from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` instead of invoking `refreshFunction`. Call sites generally assume either a `Response`-like object (then call `.json()`/`handleErrorsJson`) or a provider SDK response object (e.g., HubSpot's `createToken()`, axios responses with `.data`). Because the self-hosted endpoint returns a plain fetch Response while the provider SDK calls (e.g., hubspotClient.oauth.tokensApi.createToken, axios) return different shapes, mixing these paths behind one generic function silently breaks providers whose refresh path expects a non-fetch response shape (e.g., HubSpot, Zoho, Salesforce axios-based calls use `.data`, but the synced response is a raw Response with no `.data`).
